When a founder tells me their content feels like a mess, I usually hear one of four things."
""
"My website isn't working. My social platforms are all over the place. I'm overwhelmed with my marketing. I don't know where to start."
""
"These sound like four different problems. They're usually the same one."
""
"This is a content foundation problem."
""
"Most founders start with production. They write the website, set up the Instagram, start a newsletter. They're creating content before they've built the structure that makes content work. So everything feels disconnected, because it is."
""
"A content foundation isn't complicated. It's a small set of decisions you make once that make every content decision after it easier. Who are you talking to, specifically. What do you want them to think, feel, and do. What does your brand actually sound like in writing. How does your content connect to your business goals."
""
"Without that layer, you're not running a content strategy. You're just producing."
""
"The good news: you probably already know the answers. They just haven't been written down and handed to the work yet."
""
"If any of those four things sound familiar, DM me so we can build your foundation.

A founder sent me her pitch deck. I read it twice and still couldn't find the ask."
""
"She was looking for brand partners for a new venture. The information was all there. Her background, her vision, her audience, her credentials. Slide after slide of it."
""
"But by the time I got to the end I couldn't tell you what she was actually offering or why a brand partner should care."
""
"The deck wasn't missing information. It was missing a story."
""
"A good pitch deck isn't a comprehensive document. It's a sequence. Each slide earns the next one. The reader should feel pulled forward, not buried. When everything is included and nothing is edited out, the most important things disappear into the noise."
""
"We restructured the flow, cut what was redundant, and removed references that weren't serving the pitch. The ask became obvious. The story went from A to Z without detours."
""
"She had everything she needed. It just wasn't in the right order."
""
"If your deck covers everything but isn't landing, the problem probably isn't what's missing. It's what needs to come out.

This one question changed the entire direction of a website project. "
""
"I was talking to a founder yesterday about a website refresh. She runs a marketing agency."
""
"I asked who she was trying to reach. She said "luxury and affluent companies.""
""
"I pushed. Are there specific kinds of businesses within that world that you want to be targeting, ones you've started attracting or really want to?"
""
"She paused. Then: "Actually yes. Hospitality groups, venues, and production houses. And I've moved away from solopreneurs entirely.""
""
"That's a completely different website than the one we would have written sixty seconds earlier."
""
"She knew exactly who she wanted. She just hadn't been asked. And if I had gone straight to writing, her new site would have spoken to everyone in the luxury space and stood out to no one."
""
"This is what I mean when I say most website problems aren't writing problems. They're clarity problems that show up in the writing."
""
"Before you refresh your copy, can you answer this: not broadly who you serve, but specifically who you want more of right now?

I was hired to write quiz results copy for a job search startup. That was the brief."
""
"Two and a half years later I had built the entire content operation."
""
"Here's how it actually happened."
""
"The first thing I did was audit what existed. I asked who they were talking to, what they were trying to say, and why it mattered. What I found was a product that needed words but had no foundation to put them on. No voice. No strategy. No system."
""
"So I built one. Voice and tone guide first. Then a messaging framework and audience positioning. Then we had something to work from."
""
"The scope kept expanding the way it does at startups. MVP launch meant organic social, a paid ad campaign, and email. Then a blog. Then a LinkedIn newsletter."
""
"Then we started automating. AI-powered resume builder. Personalized outreach messaging at scale. Copy that had to work inside a product for thousands of different users without sounding like it was written by a machine."
""
"By the end it was infrastructure. A system that knew what to say, to whom, in what voice, across every surface. Built to scale as the company grew."
""
"Where are you in this? Do you have the foundation, or are you still writing copy ad hoc?

A single idea can live in ten places. But it often only lives in one. That's a waste."
""
"Write a LinkedIn post. Get traction. Archive it. Start over next week."
""
"Call it a flywheel, a repurposing system, a content engine. The name doesn't matter. The idea is the same: one piece of content is never just one piece of content."
""
"When something works, redistribute it."
""
"A LinkedIn post that got real engagement is a section of your next newsletter. That newsletter section is a talking point for your next podcast appearance. That talking point, sharpened and expanded, is a page on your website. That page, stripped back to its core idea, is three more LinkedIn posts."
""
"One idea. Multiple surfaces. Compounding reach without compounding effort."
""
"The founders who seem to be everywhere are thinking in systems. They know a good idea doesn't expire after one post. It just needs a new entry point for a different audience."
""
"The question isn't "what should I post this week." It's "what have I already said that's worth saying again, somewhere else, to someone new.""
""
"What's the best thing you've written in the last six months that most of your audience never saw?

The best feedback I've ever gotten came as an unsolicited email before I'd even sent the invoice."
""
"I got hired to help a client's client find her brand voice. I ran the discovery calls, asked the questions, listened for the patterns. The client who hired me was in the room for all of it, watching the process unfold."
""
"When I delivered the brand voice and tone system, the room got quiet for a second."
""
"Then the email came."
""
"Not a reply to an invoice. Not a "thanks, looks good." A real email. The kind where someone is typing faster than they're thinking. She wanted me to build one of these for every client in her portfolio. And one for her own business too."
""
"I was floored. And then I was confused."
""
"Because I assumed she already had one."
""
"She had a strong voice across her brand. It just lived in her head."
""
"Once it was written down, her writers could actually use it. The system went straight to her team for this specific client and the copy got noticeably better, fast."
""
"That's the thing about brand voice. It doesn't feel urgent until someone writes it down and hands it to the people doing the work. Then it feels like the thing you should have built first."
""
"If your brand voice lives in your head, it dies the moment someone else writes a word on your behalf. Do yourself and your team a favor and write it down somewhere so others can use it.

Writing my own messaging was the hardest brief I've ever taken on."
""
"I had too much to work with. Nonprofits. Policy work. UC Berkeley. Tech startups. UX copy. Content systems. AI automation. A career that made complete sense to me and looked like a different résumé every time someone else read it."
""
"So I did the only thing that actually works. I talked about it. Over and over again. To other founders, to clients, to friends, to my family. I said it differently every time and watched what landed. What made someone nod. What made someone ask a follow-up question. What made my mom say "oh, so you do X" in a way that told me I'd finally gotten it right. (A big thanks to all of these folks who let me go on and on ad nauseam. 😅) "
""
"After enough conversations, the noise fell away and one sentence was left standing. Six words. Took about six months of talking to get there."
""
"Messaging doesn't get clear at a desk. It gets clear out loud."
""
"Say it to ten different people and listen for the version that makes them lean in."
""
"That's your sentence.

Your homepage was written by the person who knows your product best. That's probably why it isn't converting."
""
"Before: A SaaS homepage that explained the product in four paragraphs and buried the value prop on paragraph three."
""
"After: A single line above the fold that told the exact customer precisely what changed when they used it."
""
"The rewrite took one week. The before/after wasn't dramatic on the surface. Same product. Same features. Completely different entry point."
""
"The work isn't inventing something new. It's finding the one true thing that was already there and putting it where people can see it."
""
"Proximity is often the problem. When you know your product inside out, you write for someone who already understands it. But a stranger landing on your homepage has three seconds and zero context. They need to see themselves in it immediately or they're gone."
""
"Sometimes you need someone who comes in not knowing anything, and notices exactly what's missing."
""
"What does your homepage say above the fold right now?

Confusing copy isn't just an aesthetic problem. It's a revenue problem."
""
"When a visitor lands on your site and can't immediately answer "what does this company do and is it for me," they leave. Not because they weren't interested. Because you made them work too hard to find out."
""
"Here's what unclear messaging actually costs:"
""
"Higher bounce rates on pages you're paying to drive traffic to. Sales calls with people who weren't a fit to begin with. A longer sales cycle because prospects don't arrive pre-convinced."
""
"The fix isn't usually a full rebrand. It's almost always a positioning problem upstream of the copy. Once that's clear, the words get easier."
""
"Clarity isn't a nice-to-have. It's the thing your conversion rate runs on.

Somewhere between the first draft and final approval, the user disappears."
""
"The draft goes into review. Someone asks for more context. Someone else wants to add a qualifier. A third person flags that it doesn't mention the thing they worked really hard on. By the time it's approved, the copy covers everything and speaks to no one."
""
"That's copy written for the room it was approved in, not the person it's supposed to reach."
""
"Copy written for internal approval sounds comprehensive, defensible, and completely forgettable. Copy written for the user stops them mid-scroll."
""
"The goal isn't to throw out the business objective. It's to reach it by a different route. When copy speaks directly to what a user actually needs, fears, or wants, it converts. And conversion is the business goal."
""
"Writing for one person specifically is what makes it work for many."
""
"The next time you're reviewing copy, ask yourself: is this being softened because it's clearer, or because it's safer?"
""
"Clearer wins. Every time.

You're already sitting on a month of content. You just don't know it yet."
""
"Many founders I talk to say the same thing: I don't know what to post. I don't have time to create content from scratch every week."
""
"The content already exists. The problem is knowing where to look."
""
"Check your sent folder. Find the last email where you explained your product to a prospect. The one where you laid out exactly why it matters, who it's for, and what changes when they use it. That email is a LinkedIn post. It's probably three of them."
""
"Check your Slack. Find the message where you explained a decision to your team. Why you chose one direction over another. What you were optimizing for. That's a post."
""
"Check your last sales call transcript. Find the moment where you said something and the other person said "wait, say that again." Whatever came out of your mouth right then is your best hook."
""
"This is a retrieval problem, not a production problem."
""
"Pick one. Sent folder, Slack, or last sales call. Go find the post that's already there.

Posting consistently but not seeing results? You might have a calendar. What you need is a strategy."
""
"A content calendar and a content strategy are not the same thing. Treating them as the same thing is one of the most common reasons content stops working."
""
"Here's the difference:"
""
"A content calendar is the execution layer. It tracks your posts, schedule, hooks, copy, visuals, and analytics. It's the what and when."
""
"A content strategy is what you build before any of that. It answers:"
""
"- What kinds of posts will you write, and in what ratio?"
"- How often will you post, and when?"
"- What's the structure of each post?"
"- What topics actually connect to your goals?"
"- What does success look like, and how will you measure it?"
""
"Without strategy, a calendar is just a schedule. You're posting consistently but not purposefully."
""
"With even a light strategy behind it, every piece of content connects to a goal. You can measure what's working, cut what isn't, and build on what lands."
""
"If you've been posting without a plan, save this for when you're ready to build one.

I did a content audit for a client and found three different brands across their website, social channels, and emails. None of them were the right one."
""
"They came to me because they wanted higher-paying clients and couldn't figure out why it wasn't happening."
""
"The answer was in the content."
""
"Their website, social channels, and client emails were all written in different voices: siloed, inconsistent, and too casual for the audience they were trying to reach. We're talking "Oops, I did it again" and "lol" energy on a site pitching premium services."
""
"They thought that kind of language felt human. And I get it. Nobody wants to sound like a corporate robot."
""
"But there's a version of human that's warm and elevated. Informal isn't the only alternative to stiff."
""
"Here's what the audit surfaced:"
""
"- Pages with redundant sections that didn't clearly explain their offerings"
"- SEO that was basically nonexistent"
"- Three different brand voices across three channels, none of them consistent"
""
"I delivered a detailed report with page-by-page feedback and specific recommendations for improvement. From there, we built a voice and tone guide from scratch. They used both to update copy across every channel. The writing got sharper, more consistent, and actually matched the clients they wanted in the room."
""
"Curious what a content audit looks at? Drop a comment or DM me. Happy to walk you through it.

I inherited a website rewrite that a previous copywriter had already botched. Here's the first thing I did."
""
"I asked why it wasn't working."
""
"The copy described what the company did. That was it. No emotional hook, no pain points addressed, no sense of who they were actually talking to."
"Before I wrote a single word, I asked:"
""
"- Who is the intended audience?"
"- What keeps them up at night?"
"- What problem is this company solving, and how?"
"- What are competitors doing?"
"- Is there an existing voice and tone guide?"
""
"That context changed everything. I wasn't just rewriting pages. I was reorienting the entire message around the reader."
""
"The result: copy across all pages delivered on time, handed off to engineering on schedule, and a client who was genuinely delighted with the outcome."
""
"Good content starts with the right questions."
""
"When was the last time someone asked you these questions before touching your website copy?

I have silently moved through life rewriting everything I’ve ever read."
""
"Bumper stickers. Billboards. Emails."
""
"Oops, that could have used a comma. Ew, look at that dangling clause."
""
"I can't help it. I'm the daughter of an English teacher. She raised me on red pen corrections and I never stood a chance."
""
"When I was older and had to write essays for school, my mom never just fixed my words. She'd circle sections of the page and say: "Try this again.""
""
"That was my cue to go back and write a better second, third, fourth draft."
""
"So I learned early that writing isn't just about getting the words right. It's about the choices you make, what to include, what to leave out, how you frame things. I became obsessed with every last word. I loved it."
""
"What I didn't realize was that I was developing something bigger than writing skills. I was developing strategy skills that would follow me everywhere."
""
"As a comms officer, I worked for nonprofits in Israel and DC shedding light on minority religions. In grad school, I wrote policy memos and presentations. As a research director at UC Berkeley, I helped political scientists and economists translate complex findings into digestible 2-pagers, the kind that policymakers in far-away countries could actually use to change their citizens' lives. "
""
"Later, I moved into tech, where at a job search startup I wrote UX copy for products used by real humans trying to find work, built content marketing programs from the ground up, and started experimenting with AI automation before most teams knew why it mattered."
""
"Different contexts. Different content. Same through line."
""
"The goal is always to communicate effectively with another human being. The only reason something gets written is to share it with someone else. Keep that front of mind and everything else (the strategy, the structure, the copy) falls into place."
""
"I've had a varied career, but I've come to see that as an asset. Every role sharpened a different part of how I think about content."
""
"That's why I built Spellwell."

AI won't fix your content problem."
""
"I know, I know. The number of posts about this is deafening. But hear me out."
""
"The promise is tempting. Plug in a prompt, get a blog post, a caption, a landing page. Done. Except it's not done. It's just fast."
""
"Here's what I've noticed: the quality of what comes out of an AI tool is directly tied to the quality of what goes in. And writing a good prompt? That's a writing skill. If you're not a strong writer, your prompts will reflect that. And so will your output."
""
"That's why handing content off to someone who isn't a writer and telling them to use AI doesn't work. The tool is only as good as the person using it."
""
"AI is genuinely powerful when a skilled person is driving. I use it every day as a thought partner, to pressure test ideas, to spot inconsistencies, to tighten something I've written that's gone a bit stream of consciousness. It's incredibly useful when you're staring at a blank page. It can help you get unstuck fast."
""
"But it doesn't replace the person who knows what to say, to whom, and why it matters."
""
"Strategy, voice, clarity, the ability to find the one true detail that stops someone cold? That's still a human job."
""
"Take a look at your last piece of AI-assisted content. Can you tell? Could your audience?

""

""
"He spent weeks researching the new Rolls-Royce, reading technical manuals, engineering reports, and automotive reviews, and settled on this line: "At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock.""
""
"No superlatives. No "luxury redefined." Just one specific, sensory, completely true detail. It killed. I think sales went up something like 50%."
